blindSummary:
This country is a very safe destination for transgender visitors. Official guidance prepared for the 2026 WorldPride hosted in the capital confirms there are no visa or entry restrictions based on gender identity, passports with amended or "X" gender markers are accepted, and no medical documentation is needed. Discrimination based on gender identity is prohibited by law, and a 2025 law makes discriminatory motive an aggravating factor that can increase penalties by a third.

The country's institutions are strongly supportive: the capital operates dedicated LGBTQIA+ reporting networks, and the mayor and police committed to priority investigation of Pride-period incidents in 2026. The capital is among the region's safer big cities for ordinary crime.

One caution: reported discrimination and violence against LGBTQ people has risen sharply since 2022 (anti-trans reports rose about 50% in the last year), and surveys indicate many queer residents avoid public displays of affection. For a visitor this translates mainly to a risk of harassment or verbal abuse, particularly late at night, rather than systematic danger.
blindOutOfScope: Pickpocketing, bike theft, and taxi scams in the capital affect all tourists.
blindSourceSummaries: Safety and travel-information page for the 2026 WorldPride host city: border/airport procedures, passport rules of the regional visa-free area, main-airport logistics, city caution, and a dedicated section for transgender and non-binary visitors; notes an external regional legal-rights index places this country's laws in the upper middle of regional peers.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): progressive laws with gaps - legal gender change still requires a medical expert letter; 'X' marker only via a 3-9 month court procedure; the self-ID gender law was withdrawn in July 2025; compensation offered to those sterilised under previous rules.

Official government page on combating discrimination and violence against LGBTIQ+ people: in 2022 one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation; over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence (17% of trans people, 22% of intersex people); verbal abuse, intimidation and violence increased sharply per the 2023 national anti-discrimination programme; lists government measures.

Government overview of new justice and security laws from 1 July 2025 - includes expansion of victims' rights and protection of victim data in criminal case records (general context, not trans-specific).

Crowd-sourced safety data: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change legal but requires medical diagnosis, nonbinary recognised, hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only, discrimination illegal, employment/housing discrimination prohibited on SOGI, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. High public support (52% support LGBT openness; among the top-rated of 121 surveyed regions as a 'good place').

National news site (April 2026): reports of discrimination targeting LGBTQ people jumped 81% since 2022 (4,800 reports last year, +7.5% vs 2024); reports about trans people specifically rose 51% in a year (264 to 399); the leading national LGBTIQ organisation called it 'extremely worrying', noting only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination last year.

National news site (July 2026): more than 70 people reported discrimination during the start of WorldPride in the capital (via an independent reporting platform) - most from festival-goers leaving a large open-air dance festival and Pride Walk participants; the platform fears the reports are 'only a fraction of the total'; safer spaces set up in hotels, museums and public buildings.

National news site (June 2026): the capital broadened reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence during WorldPride - 'Safer Spaces' across the city (a central-square church, a major art museum, the city archive, hotels) plus a central platform location; incidents to be investigated with priority; 1.4 million visitors expected.

National news site (June 2026): the capital will tackle discrimination and violent incidents with priority during WorldPride - the mayor's letter to the council; police, prosecutor and organiser agreements to act quickly; recent Prides saw 25-45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports.

Regional security-organisation page on this country's hate-crime frameworks: national legislation contains no definition of hate crime; police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents.

National government 'LGBT and gender-equality policy plan 2011-2015' (regional council repository): the cabinet's policy - combating discrimination and penalising it more severely, increasing safety so same-sex couples can walk hand-in-hand and young people can come out safely, and furthering women's labour-market participation.
blindLocalsOnly: The legal gender recognition process (still requires an expert letter, falling short of self-determination; the self-ID gender law was withdrawn in July 2025 though debate restarted in December) and the non-binary X court procedure are resident-facing.
